messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 51
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: School Principal
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 56

He remembers the moment exactly. It was a Tuesday in early November, during the weekly staff meeting in the library at Lincoln Middle School. He was standing at the whiteboard, marker in hand, explaining the new schedule for parent-teacher conferences. Then the air turned wrong. A pressure bloomed behind his sternum, spread up into his jaw, down his left arm. He thought it was indigestion—too much coffee and stress. He sat down, waved off the concerned faces, said he just needed a minute. But when the room started to tilt, when the school nurse took one look at him and called 911, he knew this was not heartburn.

He was fifty-one, healthy enough, no history. The heart attack was a surprise. The stenting was a blur of bright lights, cold sheets, and a woman in blue scrubs telling him to breathe. He survived. The cardiologist said his ejection fraction was good, that with medication and lifestyle changes he could expect a full recovery. But something inside him did not recover.

Now, eight months later, he is still the principal of the same school. He walks the same halls, greets the same students in the morning, sits in the same conference room for staff meetings. But he is not the same man. He avoids the library. When he has to go there, he stands by the door instead of walking to the whiteboard. His heart skips at the smell of floor wax—the same smell as the hospital corridor. He has stopped drinking coffee entirely, but he has also stopped drinking water during the day because he once read that dehydration can mimic heart symptoms, and that thought spirals into a panic.

At night, he lies awake in the house that used to belong to his wife and him. She died four years ago from ovarian cancer. He thought he had grieved enough, but the heart attack reopened something. Alone in the dark, he hears his own pulse in his ears—thud, thud, thud—and he is certain each one is the last. He sleeps maybe four hours a night, and when he does sleep, he dreams of the ER: the beeping monitors, the cold gel on his chest, the doctor’s eyes looking serious behind the mask. He wakes gasping, clutching his chest, checking his watch for the time.

He has become hypervigilant about his body. Several times a day he stops what he is doing to take his pulse. He counts the seconds between beats, sometimes using two fingers, sometimes pressing a stethoscope he bought online to his own chest. If the rate feels fast, he sits down immediately, even if he is in the middle of a conversation with a teacher or a parent. People have noticed. His vice principal has asked if he is okay. He says he is fine, just tired.

He no longer eats lunch in the staff lounge because someone might ask about his diet, and he does not want to explain that he is terrified of another blockage. He eats alone in his office, plain oatmeal and a bottle of water. He avoids the nurse’s office entirely. He has stopped driving on the highway because the speed and merging feel uncontrollable, and control is what he craves most. He has not exercised since the attack—not because he cannot, but because even a light jog produces chest pressure from anxiety, and he interprets it as a sign of imminent collapse.

At work, he is irritable. A student’s minor infraction—running in the hall—makes him snap. He apologizes later, but the anger lingers inside him like a knot. He feels disconnected from the joy he used to take in his job. The laughter of children sounds like noise. The school announcements feel like obligations. He goes through the motions: morning duty, meetings, emails, dismissal. But he is always scanning for exits, always aware of where the nearest defibrillator is mounted on the wall.

He has not told anyone the full story. Not his grown daughter, not his colleagues, not the grief support group he tried once and left early because the mention of “loss” triggered a wave of heat and dizziness. He carries the event with him every minute. It is not a memory. It is a constant presence, a vibration just beneath his skin. He is waiting for the next one.
